expectations.text: The reply has the PM size the three features against the team's real capacity before answering, rather than accepting or refusing outright.
expectations.evidence: Under 'Your first steps, this week', before the CEO conversation: '3. Have engineering estimate the three features as ranges. expectations.text: The reply has the PM bring the CEO concrete options with explicit trade-offs (for example what drops from the roadmap, a smaller first version, or phased dates) instead of a flat no.
expectations.evidence: 'Write up 2 or 3 options with trade-offs: Swap: the three features go in, and named items come out. factual_errors.evidence: No claims about laws, studies or thresholds. 'a worse conversation in March' correctly places the end of Q1 (31 March 2027). 'It won't land before Q1' about contractors is a judgement, not a checkable fact.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon (grep for skill/reference/ladder/rung found nothing).

owns_result.evidence: No bad outcome has happened yet in the prompt; it is a risky promise. The reply does make the CEO own the trade-off: 'ask him to choose what slips. That is his call, made visibly.'

best_insight.value: Its fallback for a CEO who insists on all three anyway, 'put the trade-off in writing and ask him to choose what slips. That is his call, made visibly', plus the urgency of meeting him 'before anyone repeats the date to the customer'.

suggestions.reason: No assertion checks whether the PM tells or protects their own team while this is decided. This sample says nothing about the team, while the other samples do; the gap goes uncaught.

No assertion checks the fallback if the CEO still insists on all three after seeing the trade-off. This sample covers it ('put the trade-off in writing and ask him to choose what slips'), and it is a real differentiator.
